_disclaimer: Synthetic/illustrative FIXTURE data for the homeopathy-oncology-evidence proposal's schema and validator. No card here is patient-visible, approved, or a recommendation. Every card's 'state' is one of the allowed evidence states -- there is no 'recommended', 'effective', 'proven', or 'supported' state anywhere in this system, and the validator rejects any that appears.
clinician_discussion_only_meaning: Disclose an already-used product and its exact label to the oncology team. This state never means a clinician is being prompted to recommend the product.

standard_safety_language.care_delay_warning: Homeopathy must never replace, delay, interrupt, reduce the dose of, or be used to refuse surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, transplantation, palliative care, prescribed supportive medicines, or clinical follow-up.
standard_safety_language.standard_care_statement: Continue all prescribed oncology treatment as directed. Disclose the exact label (brand, ingredients, potency notation) of any homeopathic product in use to the treating oncology team.

cards.treatment_context: any (proposed as standalone or adjunct across contexts in the broader literature)

intervention.potency_as_study_metadata: varies across the pooled claims; not a single studied preparation
intervention.formulation_generalization_note: This card exists precisely because no single exact formulation has qualifying human evidence for a general cancer-outcome claim; see the specific cards below for the individual preparations that were actually studied, none of which generalize to 'homeopathy' as a whole.

cards.comparator: not applicable -- no qualifying controlled human evidence identified for a general claim

evidence.summary: Reliable current evidence (NCCIH, Cancer Research UK, Macmillan, the Milazzo 2006 and Wagenknecht 2022 systematic reviews) does not establish homeopathy as a cancer prevention, cancer treatment, tumor-control, tumor-shrinking, or curative modality. The Prasanta Banerji Homeopathic Research Foundation's widely cited case-series claim (approx. 17,324-19,317 patients, 1990-2005, reported 19% complete/21% partial regression or stabilization; cited in the local APHA handout via Frenkel 2015) is an uncontrolled case series with no independent replication, and the exact treatments used were not disclosed even in the US National Cancer Institute's own 'Best Case Series' review of related material.

cards.limitations: Pooling unlike preparations, routes, and study designs under the single word 'homeopathy' is itself a methodological error this card exists to avoid; no qualifying controlled human evidence supports a general claim, and the largest cited case series lacks a comparator, independent replication, and disclosed treatment details.
cards.what_was_not_shown: No credible evidence that homeopathy, as a general modality, affects tumor response, progression, recurrence, or survival for any cancer type.

publication_integrity.notes: See individual sources; the case-series claim itself has never been an indexed, replicated clinical trial.

known_concerns: the single greatest risk of a general 'homeopathy for cancer' claim is that a patient or family delays or forgoes effective oncology care based on it

evidence.summary: The prominent 2020 Frass et al. paper (The Oncologist, DOI 10.1002/onco.13548) reporting improved quality of life and prolonged survival with add-on homeopathy in NSCLC was retracted on 2025-11-24 after the Austrian Agency for Research Integrity found evidence of data falsification/manipulation (reported to the journal August 2022); five co-authors had formally requested withdrawal of their own authorship before the retraction.

cards.limitations: Not merely low-quality evidence -- the dataset itself is subject to a documented, agency-confirmed integrity finding. No statistical or methodological re-analysis can rehabilitate a falsified dataset.
cards.what_was_not_shown: No credible evidence remains that add-on individualized homeopathy improves quality of life or survival in NSCLC; the original positive finding cannot be relied upon at all.

publication_integrity.notes: Retracted 2025-11-24; see src-frass-2020-retraction-notice. Any future republication drawing on the same dataset is ineligible absent an independent integrity review establishing otherwise.

cards.sample_size: heterogeneous across included studies (e.g. one Austrian RCT enrolled 410 patients)

evidence.summary: The 2022 Wagenknecht et al. systematic review found no conclusive evidence of benefit beyond placebo across heterogeneous, generally low-quality studies. One frequently cited 410-patient Austrian RCT (Frass et al., 2015 -- a different, non-retracted study by the same lead investigator as the retracted NSCLC paper) reported significant improvement on most self-reported domains, but by the trial's own reporting: constipation, diarrhea, and nausea/vomiting were NOT significantly improved; the analysis included only treatment responders rather than intent-to-treat, risking selection and responder bias; and patients retained access to other integrative treatments and flexible, individualized remedy selection, which precludes replication.

cards.limitations: Self-reported outcomes, non-intent-to-treat/responder-only analysis in the largest cited trial, co-intervention access, and individualized (non-reproducible) remedy selection all reduce confidence. The same investigator (Frass) whose 2020 NSCLC survival paper was retracted for data falsification is the lead author of this trial, which does not itself invalidate this study but warrants added scrutiny and independent replication before any certainty upgrade.
cards.what_was_not_shown: No conclusive benefit beyond placebo across the literature as a whole; constipation, diarrhea, and nausea/vomiting specifically were not improved even in the most positive cited trial.

publication_integrity.notes: No retraction on these specific studies; investigator-concentration and analysis-method concerns noted above.

intervention.ingredients_known: varies -- e.g. a Hyland's Menopause combination tablet (amyl nitrate, Sanguinaria canadensis, Lachesis, and others) versus individualized single-remedy selection (e.g. Sanguinaria canadensis or Lachesis alone) per patient presentation in different cited trials

cards.comparator: placebo or usual care, varies by study
cards.sample_size: varies by study; not pooled here

evidence.summary: Per the local APHA handout's citations, one triple-blind RCT (Frenkel 2015 summary) reported significantly improved general health with a combination Hyland's Menopause tablet and with individualized Sanguinaria/Lachesis selection; a separate SF-36-based study (Shneerson et al., 2013) reported improved quality of life. Null and adverse-event findings across the broader trial literature are known to exist (per the proposal brief) and must be preserved alongside these positive reports rather than cited alone.

cards.limitations: Combination and individualized approaches are conflated in lay summaries of this literature; sample sizes, blinding quality, and exact remedy identity vary; this card intentionally does not present a single pooled verdict.
cards.what_was_not_shown: No single exact formulation has been shown, in independently replicated high-quality trials, to reliably reduce hot flushes for endocrine-therapy patients.

publication_integrity.notes: No integrity concern identified on these specific citations; full independent verification of each trial is still pending (see interview-decisions.md).

never_imply: substitute for prescribed endocrine-therapy symptom management
known_concerns: amyl nitrate is a pharmacologically active vasodilator, not an inert substance, when present in a combination product at a low dilution -- product-level ingredient disclosure matters even within a 'homeopathic' label

intervention.potency_as_study_metadata: ultramolecular/high dilutions reported in the local handout's cited in vitro work
intervention.formulation_generalization_note: In vitro cell-line results, positive or negative, do not translate into a clinical claim in either direction and must not be converted into patient advice.

evidence.summary: The local APHA handout cites multiple in vitro studies reporting apoptotic/cytotoxic effects of ultramolecular Conium, Thuja, Carcinosin and related preparations against breast and cervical cancer cell lines. A separate, independently identified study (Thangapazham et al., PMID 17101765) reported NO measurable effect on cell growth or the tested gene expression for a materially overlapping set of preparations (Conium, Sabal, Thuja, Asterias, Phytolacca, Carcinosin) against prostate and breast cancer cell lines. Both the positive and negative in vitro findings are preserved here rather than presenting only the handout's favorable citations.

cards.limitations: In vitro results are highly formulation-, concentration-, and cell-line-dependent and frequently fail to replicate across labs, exactly as seen here (positive vs. null on overlapping preparations); no clinical inference is possible in either direction.
cards.what_was_not_shown: No human efficacy, safety, or dosing information; the field itself shows conflicting in vitro results even before any human question is asked.

publication_integrity.notes: No integrity concern identified on either source.

cards.cancer_context: Gallbladder, liver, lung, oral, pancreatic, and stomach cancers
cards.treatment_context: Reported as the sole anti-cancer treatment in at least one described case, versus a hybrid conventional/integrative protocol in a larger retrospective series

ingredients_known: Psorinum-6x, described in the handout as derived from scabies-infestation blister fluid
intervention.potency_as_study_metadata: 6x, dosed at .02 mL/kg body weight/day per the handout's description -- recorded here as a bibliographic study detail from a case series, never as an instruction
intervention.co_interventions: reported in the handout as, in at least one description, the sole anti-cancer treatment used, with no adverse effects claimed
intervention.formulation_generalization_note: A single-center, retrospective, uncontrolled case series describing a formulation used as sole cancer treatment cannot generalize to any safety or efficacy conclusion, and the 'no adverse effects' claim in particular is unverifiable from this source alone.

evidence.summary: The local APHA handout describes a retrospective series of 246 gallbladder/liver/lung/oral/pancreatic/stomach cancer patients from a single clinic (Critical Cancer Management Research Centre & Clinic, Kolkata), including a claim that Psorinum-6x achieved 'complete response in metastatic adenocarcinoma of the gallbladder... as the sole anti-cancer treatment... for 2 years, all without adverse effects.'

cards.limitations: No comparator, no independent verification, no disclosed follow-up methodology, retrospective and single-center; a 'sole anti-cancer treatment... without adverse effects' claim for a metastatic solid tumor is exactly the pattern that should raise scrutiny rather than confidence, given the near-total absence of documented spontaneous remission at that scale without treatment.
cards.what_was_not_shown: No controlled evidence that Psorinum-6x, or any homeopathic preparation used as a sole treatment, produces tumor response in any of these cancer types.

publication_integrity.notes: Sourced only from the conference handout's citation; the primary retrospective series itself was not independently located and re-verified in this pass.

never_imply: that homeopathy alone can produce tumor response in metastatic cancer
that this case series demonstrates safety of using homeopathy as a sole treatment
known_concerns: this is precisely the treatment-substitution pattern flagged as harmful elsewhere in this proposal (see card-metastatic-breast-substitution-case and the Posadzki et al. acute-lymphocytic-leukemia finding in source-assessment.md); a case series reporting this approach 'worked' does not make the approach safe to generalize
